This is NPR News Now. The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Giles Snyder. Heartbroken and horrified. The school superintendent and
Bend Oregon's Stephen Cook describing what the Bend community is going through tonight after a
gunman killed three children and a teacher at an elementary school. This is the kind of thing you
hear about in other places and pray that it never happens here and it has happened here.
The children killed were age 5, 8, and 11 and in addition to the teacher killed another student
and teacher were injured and taken to a hospital. Police say the gunman was 16 years old and he was
killed by an armed member of the community who had pursued him into the school. The Justice
Department suing California to block state election officials from counting mail-in ballots
from suspected non-citizens and peers Ryan Lucas reports. The Justice Department says it filed its
lawsuit after election officials in California failed to cross-check the state's voter rolls
against a list of some 20,000 names of quote-unquote likely non-citizens believed to have been sent vote
by mail ballots. The DOJ provided that list of names to state election officials earlier this week
on an encrypted thumb drive and gave them a 48-hour deadline to conduct a review.
In its lawsuit the department is asking the court to block California from counting mail-in ballots
from what it calls likely non-citizens until voter citizenship can be determined. California's
Secretary of State rejected the DOJ's efforts saying this week the department is trying to
unlawfully access protected voter data. Ryan Lucas, NPR News, Washington. FBI employees fired
for their rolls in the investigation of President Trump's retention of classified documents at his
Florida state are suing to get their jobs back. Their complaint filed Thursday calls their
termination unlawful acts of political retribution. The suit was filed in federal court in Washington,
D.C. on behalf of nine agents, intelligence analysts, and staff operations specialists.
FBI Director Cash Patel says employees he has fired had weaponized the FBI.
Rising inflation adding to the strain on household budgets, NPR's Winston Johnson reports that
people across the U.S. have collectively spent about 82 billion dollars more on gasoline since
March than they did a year ago. That estimate comes from the latest calculation by gasbuddy.com.
Patrick DeHaan is head of petroleum analysis. He says those extra fuel expenses are leaving
families with less to spend on holiday meals and gifts. He also says booking holiday flights now
won't spare travelers from higher fuel costs. Airlines are having to pass this along. So,
you know, you can't avoid the increase in fuel when what comes out of a barrel is fueling the
entire U.S. economy. You can't escape it. Heavy, bulky goods including Thanksgiving turkeys and
perishable foods are especially vulnerable to higher shipping costs. Winston Johnson, NPR News.
This is NPR News.
Pope Leo has resumed working. The Vatican says Leo met Thursday with a top aide and resumed his
duties while hospitalized following lung surgery Tuesday to remove a cancerous nodule. Leo's
doctor says his post-operative tests are normal and he is independently going about daily activities.
He is expected to remain hospitalized until at least October 20th. Schools across the country
are looking for ways to embrace artificial intelligence but there's little research or
policy to guide them. Lee Gaines reports that many educators are experimenting with AI to figure out
what works and what doesn't. A San Diego charter school recently introduced students to an AI-powered
humanoid robot. In some districts, AI gives students feedback on their work and the public
school district in Dayton, Ohio recently piloted a social-emotional AI chatbot designed to help
students open up about their feelings. While I live in the West, it feels very Wild West in terms of
the randomness. Robin Lake is the director of the Center on Reinventing Public Education which has
been tracking AI adoption in schools. There are so many questions. This is bigger than individual
schools. Even individual districts can figure out on their own. We need state and federal leadership.
But for now, she says, states and the federal government have been mostly hands-off.
For NPR News, I'm Lee Gaines. Asian shares advancing in Friday trading after Wall Street
